newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels unfurl banners in new show of defiance.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels unfurl banners in new show of defiance.

text.p: Peruvian Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home unfurled defiant new banners early on Saturday, breaking a mood of optimism created by talks aimed at a peaceful end to the crisis.

Under the cover of darkness, three men scurried across the roof of the diplomatic residence and draped two new banners over a side wall, according to cameramen watching the mansion with night-vision lenses from a nearby building.

"Surrender is not the way of Tupac Amaristas," read one banner in bold red letters, referring to Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) who stormed the residence 74 days ago touching off the longest hostage situation in Latin American history.
The second said: "Peruvians - remember that (President Alberto) Fujimori does not govern for the poor. Fight for your rights."

The new banners hung beside two others -- one referring to the rebels' main demand of release of some 400 jailed comrades and comparing their relatives to those of hostages, and another unreadable -- that were unfurled earlier in the siege.

The rebels stormed the residence Dec. 17, 1996, in a bid to force the government to free their comrades, whom they claim are held in inhuman conditions. They also demanded an end to Peru's secret military court system and a reorganization of the economy to benefit the poor.
Fujimori repeatedly ruled out considering the release of MRTA prisoners but indicated he might make other concessions.

The MRTA underlined their fresh defiance by hoisting a red-and-white flag emblazoned with a mace, a rifle and the image of Tupac Amaru -- an 18th century Andean Indian who led an unsuccessful, bloody uprising against Spanish colonial rule before he was executed by being drawn and quartered.
One of the men who lowered the banners covered his face with a red-and-white MRTA bandana. Another, wearing overalls, was shirtless while the third was dressed in shirt and pants, witnesses said.
Several hours after sunrise, two unarmed rebels dashed across the roof again to straighten the banners, witnesses said.
Holed up in the fortified compound and with most lines of communication cut, the MRTA has several times used banners to wage its propaganda war against the government.

But with talks between the two sides apparently making some progress, the rebels had refrained from such tactics since Jan. 23 and this week the mood was upbeat following a series of face-to-face talks.

With both sides bound to secrecy, details of the talks were scarce but mediators appeared optimistic after the last meeting on Thurdsay saying they "noted and appreciated the desire of the participants to achieve a solution."
An eighth round of talks were scheduled to begin on Monday.

Dawn broke on Saturday with the MRTA broadcasting its now common revolutionary hymn "Los Molinos" (The Mills), only to be quickly drowned out by police blaring patriotic music through loudspeakers placed outside the compound.
Later in the morning, the musical skirmishing settled down with police playing traditional Peruvian "criollo" waltzes, Mexican rancheras and soft rock.

On Friday, meanwhile, Latin America's best known human rights group gave up hope of playing a mediating role in the talks. After a week of rebuffs, a delegation of the Buenos Aires-based Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo finally announced it was going home.
Bitter at being snubbed by President Fujimori, who refused to even see the group, the Mothers' delegation said it would charge Peru with human rights abuses.

"(The Mothers) are going to present a formal complaint (to international organisations) against the Peruvian government for its prisons and political prisoners," Hebe de Bonafini, the group's leader, said.

Fujimori has said he will not use force to end the situation unless harm is done to the remaining captives, who include his brother, envoys of Japan and Bolivia, two government ministers and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
